items.stem: Al-Masūdī, a 10th-century Arab historian and traveller from Baghdad, gave high praise to a Rāṣhṭrakūṭa ruler: “His troops and elephants are innumerable. … There is none among the rulers of Sindh and Hind who in his territory respects the Muslims [as he does]. In his kingdom, Islam is honoured and protected. And, for them, mosques and congregational mosques, which are always full, have been built for offering prayers five times.”
items.answer:  This passage shows that the Rashtrakutas were powerful and militarily strong, with large armies and many elephants. They were also wealthy and well-organised. The ruler was tolerant towards different religions, especially Islam, as mosques were built and protected, allowing Muslims to practice freely. This reflects religious harmony and good governance in their kingdom.

items.stem: How does a professional group transform into a jati?
items.answer:  A professional group becomes a jati when people of the same occupation form a distinct community. Over time, they follow common customs, marry within the group, pass their profession to future generations, and develop their own social rules, thus becoming a jati.

items.stem: Sulaiman, a 9th-century Arab merchant and traveller, makes this comment on a Gurjara- Pratīhāra ruler: “This king maintains numerous forces, and no other Indian prince has so fine a cavalry. He is unfriendly to the Arabs … there is no greater foe of the Muhammadan faith than he. ... He has riches, and his camels and horses are numerous. … There is no country in India safer from robbers.” Why do you think the author calls the ruler a ‘foe to the Muslim faith’?
items.answer:  The ruler is called a “foe to the Muslim faith” because he strongly opposed the Arabs and prevented their expansion in India. His powerful army and strong cavalry made it difficult for them to defeat him, so the traveller viewed him as an enemy of their faith.

items.stem: During this period, inscriptions began using both Sanskrit and regional languages simultaneously. In land grants, the ruler and his dynastic history were often praised in Sanskrit, while the operative details of the grant were recorded in the local language. Why do you think such inscriptions were written in two languages?
items.answer:  Inscriptions were written in both Sanskrit and the local language because they served different purposes. (a) For prestige and cultural importance: Sanskrit was the language of scholars, religion, and royal courts. Its use made the king appear learned and prestigious. It was mainly used to praise the ruler and his lineage in a formal and grand manner. (b) For practical understanding: The details of land grants—such as boundaries, taxes, recipients, and duties—were written in the local language. items.stem: How did the Cholas build their empire’s prosperity?
items.answer:  The Cholas ensured deep prosperity through an efficient administration, a powerful navy, and advanced irrigation techniques that boosted the Kaveri delta’s agriculture.

items.stem: How does the development of jatis indicate a complex social structure in this era?
items.answer:  The rapid multiplication of jatis illustrates a highly complex, evolving society driven by diverse occupational and regional changes. New professional groups, like the scribal Kayasthas, gradually transformed into distinct, endogamous castes. While this rigidified certain social boundaries, it also allowed flexible integration of foreign migrants and indigenous tribal populations economically.

items.stem: Analyse the significance of Kalhana’s Rajatarangini as a historical text.
items.answer:  Kalhana’s epic Rajatarangini is historically exceptional because it meticulously utilizes ancient inscriptions, royal grants, and prior chronicles to reconstruct Kashmir’s dynastic lineage objectively. Beyond recording mere facts, Kalhana specifically aimed to extract profound moral lessons, explicitly judging whether past rulers ethically upheld order or disastrously harassed their innocent subjects.

items.stem: Discuss the importance of Vikramashila as a centre of learning under the Palas.
items.answer:  Founded by Dharmapala, Vikramashila thrived for centuries as an elite, massive university featuring six specialized colleges. It attracted thousands of international students to rigorously study advanced grammar, logic, and philosophy. Its scholars significantly shaped Vajrayana Buddhism in Tibet through dedicated translations, cementing India’s profound legacy in global knowledge traditions.

items.stem: How did the Rashtrakutas balance military expansion with cultural patronage?
items.answer:  The Rashtrakutas aggressively conquered vast territories across India, repeatedly challenging powerful northern kingdoms. Despite constant warfare, they generously funded monumental architectural marvels, notably commissioning Ellora’s magnificent rock-cut Kailashanatha temple. They fostered a rich intellectual environment by enthusiastically supporting diverse Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain scholars writing in Sanskrit and regional languages.

items.stem: Evaluate the strategic importance of the Chalukya capital, Vatapi.
items.answer:  Vatapi, the fortified Chalukya capital, served as a crucial military and cultural stronghold in the Deccan. Under Pulakeshin II, it became an impenetrable base that successfully halted Harsha’s southern expansion. Furthermore, the city fostered an incredible artistic renaissance, showcasing magnificently carved Hindu and Jain cave temples reflecting immense prosperity.

items.stem: Analyse the role of women in governance during the 6th to 10th centuries.
items.answer:  While patriarchal structures generally favored male heirs, prominent women often wielded immense political authority. Empress Tribhuvana Mahadevi I of Odisha brilliantly exemplified female leadership by ruthlessly suppressing local rebellions, exhibiting exceptional administrative prowess, and independently issuing royal land grants while proudly carrying the majestic title of supreme sovereign empress.

items.stem: How did scientific knowledge from India influence the Arab world and Europe?
items.answer:  Indian mathematical and astronomical genius, notably championed by Brahmagupta, profoundly influenced global science. Arab scholars in Baghdad actively translated these classical Sanskrit treatises, eagerly adopting India’s revolutionary decimal system and the concept of zero. These concepts were subsequently transmitted into medieval Europe, establishing the vital foundations of modern global mathematics. CASE BASED QUESTIO 

items.stem: Analyse the significance of the Tripartite Struggle in north Indian politics.
items.answer:  The Tripartite Struggle was a prolonged, centuries- long conflict involving the Palas, Gurjara- Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas fighting vigorously to control Kannauj. This strategic city symbolized immense power across the fertile Gangetic plains. However, this continuous, exhausting warfare yielded no lasting victor, ultimately fragmenting northern India and weakening these vast, powerful regional empires.

items.stem: How did the Pallava dynasty contribute to cultural and economic growth in south India?
items.answer:  The Pallavas transformed their capital Kanchi into a thriving economic hub trading in spices and silk. They constructed magnificent monolithic rock-cut temples at Mamallapuram and heavily patronised both Sanskrit and Tamil literature. Their prosperous seaports maintained extensive international maritime connections with Southeast Asia, China, and the distant Roman Empire.

items.stem: Discuss the evolution of the Bhakti tradition between the 6th and 10th centuries.
items.answer:  The Bhakti Movement emerged powerfully in south India, championed by Vishnu-worshipping Alvars and Shiva-devoted Nayanars. These passionate saints composed deeply devotional regional poetry, directly emphasizing a loving, personal relationship with God. This inclusive religious movement bypassed traditional Vedic rituals, successfully uniting diverse social layers and actively breaking rigid social barriers.

items.stem: Evaluate the impact of land grants on the social and economic structure during this period.
items.answer:  The widespread land grant system created a powerful new class of wealthy landholders while expanding agricultural cultivation immensely. Kings generously donated territories to religious institutions and royal vassals. This system boosted rural economies and cash crops through improved irrigation, but it often allowed powerful intermediaries to heavily exploit local peasants.

items.stem: Analyse the role of regional merchant guilds in the economic life of post-Gupta India.
items.answer:  Merchant guilds became highly influential organizations uniting skilled artisans, local traders, and wealthy moneylenders. They efficiently managed prosperous regional markets and aggressively drove extensive maritime commerce connecting India to Southeast Asia and the Middle East. Furthermore, these wealthy associations generously supported prominent religious institutions and vital local charitable activities.

items.stem: How did Harsha’s administration and cultural patronage reflect the ideals of ancient Indian kingship?
items.answer:  Harshavardhana exemplified ideal kingship through his energetic governance, vast military campaigns, and profound religious tolerance. He generously patronised brilliant scholars like Banabhatta and regularly held massive assemblies at Prayaga to distribute his accumulated wealth to the poor, thereby continuously fostering a vibrant, culturally rich, and highly inclusive Indian society.

items.stem: Examine the assimilation process of foreign groups like the Hunas into Indian society.
items.answer:  Initially arriving as fierce nomadic invaders, the Hunas were decisively defeated militarily. Following their defeat, they rapidly assimilated into mainstream Indian society by serving as local administrators and soldiers. They fully adopted regional languages like Sanskrit and actively embraced traditional Hindu religious symbols and royal titles on their minted coins.

items.stem: In Kalyānī, Basavanna established an anubhava mandapa (literally, ‘pavilion of experience’), where men and women from every social, economic, religious or linguistic background, including saints and philosophers, could assemble to discuss all aspects of life, including moral values and religion. (a) Why, in your opinion, did Basava want people from all backgrounds to come together and exchange ideas? (b) If something like an anubhava mandapa existed today, what important topics do you think people ought to discuss there? (c) What lessons can we draw from the anubhava mandapa spirit to create a just and civil society today?
items.answer:  (a) Basava established the Anubhava Mandapa to promote social and spiritual reform by challenging caste divisions and ritual practices. By bringing together people of all backgrounds, he emphasized the equal spiritual worth of every individual and questioned existing hierarchies. The mandapa acted as an inclusive space for sharing ideas, encouraging personal devotion (bhakti) and ethical living, while promoting equality within the Lingayat movement. (b) If a forum like the Anubhava Mandapa— open, inclusive, and non-hierarchical—existed today, discussions would likely address major social, ethical, and global challenges. It offers important lessons for building a just society by promoting inclusive dialogue, equality, and collective participation. (c) The most important lesson is radical inclusion. By bringing together people from all backgrounds, including those marginalized by caste and gender, Basava showed that real progress is possible only when every voice is heard and valued equally, regardless of status or identity. By making the mandapa a space for open ethical discussion, he emphasized that collective wisdom is stronger than top-down authority. Today, this means creating inclusive public platforms where policies and social values are shaped through open dialogue, with the experiences of the vulnerable guiding decisions rather than those of privileged elites. THINK ABOU T I 

items.stem: We will meet later in this chapter the Persian scholar al-Bīrūnī, who accompanied Mahmūd in some of his campaigns. He wrote in his memoirs on India, “The Hindu Shāhiya dynasty is now extinct, and of the whole house there is no longer the slightest remnant in existence. We must say that, in all their grandeur, they never slackened in the ardent desire of doing that which is good and right, that they were men of noble sentiment and noble bearing.” What conclusions can we draw from this remark by someone in Mahmūd’s entourage?
items.answer:  Al-Biruni’s remark suggests that although Mahmud’s forces defeated the Hindu Shahiya dynasty, the Persians who accompanied him still recognised the rulers’ strong moral and ethical values. The Shahiyas were viewed as just, principled, and honourable leaders who maintained high standards of conduct. This indicates that even in defeat, their noble character was acknowledged, showing that military victory did not prevent admiration for their virtues. NCER T EXERCIS 

items.stem: Why is the period under consideration in this chapter regarded as a major transition in Indian history? Give two examples each of change and continuity from this period.
items.answer:  It is a transition because it marks the end of purely indigenous regional struggles and the beginning of foreign Turkic rule in north India.

items.stem: In later centuries, the Somanātha temple was rebuilt and destroyed again several times; the existing temple was built in 1950 and inaugurated the next year by the then President of India, Rajendra Prasad. Why do you think it was decided to fund the construction entirely from public donations?
items.answer:  The decision to rebuild the Somnath temple using only public donations was intentional, turning it into a national, people-driven effort. Since the temple had been destroyed multiple times—most notably by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1026 CE—this approach highlighted that its importance went beyond state support, symbolising cultural and spiritual strength. It also allowed citizens to take part in its restoration, creating a sense of shared ownership and reinforcing the idea that Indian culture is enduring and resilient.

items.stem: In the painting Fig., can you make out who is the king and who is the guru? What does the king’s posture and general attitude express?
items.answer:  The figure on the left, shown in a position of respect, represents the Guru (spiritual teacher), while the figure on the right is the king, Rajendra Chola I. The king’s posture reflects humility and deep reverence. With hands in anjali mudra (a gesture of respect), a slightly bowed head, and eyes focused on the Guru, he appears attentive and devoted, receiving guidance from the seated teacher.

items.answer:  During the 11th and 12th centuries, the political landscape of India witnessed continuity, decline, and the emergence of new powers. Why do you think Mahmūd of Ghazni carry out repeated raids from Afghanistan into India, while Muhammad Ghūrī sought territorial expansion into India and long-term control? Write a short note on how their motives shaped the outcomes of their campaigns.
items.answer:  Mahmud of Ghazni’s repeated invasions were mainly driven by the desire for plunder. He aimed to seize the immense wealth of temples, such NODIA as Somnath, to fund his army and develop his capital at Ghazni. Since he had no intention of establishing lasting control beyond Punjab, his campaigns resulted in a series of destructive raids that weakened existing Indian kingdoms. In contrast, Muhammad Ghuri was focused on territorial expansion and long-term rule. After his decisive victory in the Second Battle of Tarain, he appointed his general Qutb-ud-din Aibak to secure and administer the conquered regions, including Delhi and the Gangetic plains. Therefore, Ghuri’s objective led to the establishment of a stable political authority, laying the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate. MULTIPL E CHOICE QUESTIO 
